article.title: The Trump Shock That Wasn’t (At Least Not Yet)

metadata_extension.subtitle: The “core” U.S. trade deficit is still expanding, thanks to strong electronics imports.

summary.central_question: Why has the huge Trump tariff shock to trade rules not produced a comparable shock to core trade flows and the global economy?
summary.main_thesis: The tariff shock to the trade rules has so far been much bigger than the shock to trade flows.

content.text: Why has the huge Trump tariff shock to trade rules not produced a comparable shock to core trade flows and the global economy?
content.reason: A large change in policy rules need not translate into an equally large change in economic flows.

passages.source_excerpt: The impact of the tariffs core trade flows—and hence the global economy—has been modest, at least so far.

content.text: The U.S. has moved from low, bound, MFN tariffs to high, unbound, country-specific tariffs with demanding rules of origin, a profound rejection of WTO rules.
content.reason: Abandoning bound and nondiscriminatory tariffs breaks the core commitments of a rules-based trade system.

passages.source_excerpt: All this is a profound rejection of the basic rules of the WTO—which haven’t just been rejected for trade with China, but for all trade.

reasons: boxes: `C1` the name `mfn` does not occur in the article

content.text: Tariff rates now vary by origin, from 50 percent on India and Brazil to 10 percent on the UK and Australia and zero for USMCA-compliant trade.
content.reason: Different rates on the same good by origin are direct evidence of discrimination among trading partners.

passages.source_excerpt: Importers of the same good will pay different tariffs depending on the origin of the good (50 percent for India and Brazil, 30 percent for China plus any section 301 duty, 20 percent for Vietnam

content.text: The headline reading that the tariffs have caused trade swings bigger than COVID or Lehman, and so a major shock to global trade flows, is misleading.
content.reason: Headline aggregates dominated by distorted categories can create a false impression of an underlying shock.

passages.source_excerpt: The dollar value of imports has swung by more than during COVID or the Lehman shock.

content.text: Measured U.S. imports swung more than during COVID or Lehman, and the annualized deficit went from $2 trillion to $1 trillion and back to about $1.2 trillion.
content.reason: Large swings in headline trade data show volatility but not necessarily a change in underlying trade.

passages.source_excerpt: The annualized monthly trade deficit rose to a peak of $2 trillion in March before dipping to $1 trillion and then rebounding to $1.2 trillion in July

content.text: Tax-driven pharmaceutical trade and stockpiling, together with gold flows, produce most of the headline volatility without reflecting core trade.
content.reason: Goods that are easily stockpiled or booked for tax reasons distort trade statistics and should be stripped out to see core trends.

passages.source_excerpt: pharmaceuticals (where trade is heavily distorted by tax and companies can easily front-run tariffs by stockpiling active ingredients) and gold.

reasons: boxes: `M1` the name `tax-driven` does not occur in the article

content.text: The proper measure of core trade excludes pharmaceuticals and gold, and on that measure U.S. trade looks normal.
content.reason: The categories excluded from a trade measure can decide whether a shock appears large or small.

passages.source_excerpt: Take out pharmaceuticals and gold and U.S. trade looks, well, rather normal.

reasons: links: `Q` frames `SCP` joins L0→L1B, which no hand-drawn frames link does

content.text: Imports from China collapsed while imports from Taiwan and Southeast Asia soared, leaving total imports from Asia roughly unchanged.
content.reason: Trade diversion toward lower-tariff origins can offset falls from high-tariff origins.

passages.source_excerpt: imports from China (where hefty tariffs were expected) tanked. But imports from Taiwan and Southeast Asia (which were only subject to a 10 percent tariff

content.text: Auto imports slowed, but an AI data-center investment boom has sharply raised electronics imports, with Taiwan imports up over 50 percent.
content.reason: A strong sectoral demand boom can outweigh tariff drag on overall import volumes.

passages.source_excerpt: imports of electronics are up substantially (imports from Taiwan are up over 50 percent YTD) on the back of booming investment in data centers

content.text: Global trade has held up well despite the largest importer flouting the rules.
content.reason: Once distortions are removed and the offsets are counted, aggregate trade resilience can coexist with rule-breaking.

passages.source_excerpt: So global trade has actually held up rather well even though the world’s largest economy

content.text: Record tariff revenue implies that Americans keep importing and paying the tariff, which is good news for trade partners.
content.reason: Tariff revenue equals the rate times the import base, so high revenue requires that imports continue.

passages.source_excerpt: the surge in revenue implies that Americans are continuing to import and just paying the tariff.

content.text: The August deals and letters raised tariffs sharply for many countries, to an average of about 15 percent, doubling them on Southeast Asia.
content.reason: Higher effective tariffs should eventually weigh on trade volumes.

passages.source_excerpt: tariffs on Southeast Asia doubled relative to April

reasons: passages: `E4`: the team's passage linker anchors it to p14 (shared: southeast), which the box does not cite

content.text: First-term China tariffs of about 15 percent cut bilateral trade by about 30 percent, implying a bilateral elasticity near 2.
content.reason: Past responses to tariffs give an empirical basis for estimating trade elasticities.

passages.source_excerpt: The roughly 15 percent average tariff increase on trade with China in trump’s first term reduced trade by roughly 30 percent

reasons: passages: `E5`: the team's passage linker anchors it to p7 (shared: 30percent), which the box does not cite

content.text: A bilateral elasticity overstates the effect of a global tariff because bilateral tariffs are evaded by rerouting assembly through third countries.
content.reason: Diversion inflates measured bilateral responses relative to the response to tariffs applied on all origins.

passages.source_excerpt: the bilateral tariff elasticity of 2 is too high for a global tariff increase—remember that firms shifted final assembly to southeast Asia

content.text: The exchange-rate import elasticity of 0.3 to 0.4 is the right analogue for a global tariff.
content.reason: A broad tariff raises import prices much as a currency depreciation does, so the price elasticities should be similar.

passages.source_excerpt: The import elasticity for exchange rate moves is closer to 0.3 or 0.4

content.text: Importers respond to a tariff-driven price rise the same way they respond to an equal exchange-rate-driven price rise.
content.reason: Mapping estimates from one kind of price shock to another requires the two shocks to be passed through and perceived alike.

reasons: facets: `setser_2025-09-12_trump-shock-that-wasnt#P2` where_subject empty - every claim needs a country or a bloc (assignment.requires_one_of) - needs review

content.text: A 15 percent tariff should cut U.S. imports by 5 to 6 percent, taking non-oil imports from about 10 to 9.5 percent of GDP: meaningful, but far smaller than COVID or the global financial crisis.
content.reason: Multiplying the price shock by an appropriate elasticity gives a bounded estimate of the volume effect.

passages.source_excerpt: so a 15 percent tariff might be expected to reduce impacts by 5-6 percent. That is a year or two of normal import volume growth

content.text: Some exporters can offset lost U.S. sales by taking market share from U.S. exporters, who face higher input costs.
content.reason: Tariffs on inputs raise the costs of domestic exporters and cede third markets to foreign rivals.

passages.source_excerpt: Some countries will be able to offset reduced U.S. sales by taking market share from US exports

content.text: There is little sign yet of the expected effect: U.S. imports are on trend and high-frequency global trade measures have not slowed.
content.reason: Current data should be compared against the predicted effect to judge whether that effect has materialized.

passages.source_excerpt: U.S. imports are, more or less, on trend (with front-running pulling imports forward to Q1 just a bit).

content.text: The tariff shock to the trade rules has so far been much bigger than the shock to trade flows.
content.reason: Policy regime change and its measured economic impact must be assessed separately.

passages.source_excerpt: The liberation day shock to the trade rules was thus bigger than the shock to overall trade flows.

content.text: The conclusion is provisional: the fall data should show a larger impact than is visible now.
content.reason: Trade responds to price shocks with lags, so early readings understate the eventual effect.

passages.source_excerpt: there should be more of an impact than is now apparent.

content.text: The analogy is imperfect: a depreciation also boosts exports, whereas a tariff does not.
content.reason: Analogies between policy instruments hold only for the channels they share.

passages.source_excerpt: An actual exchange rate depreciation increases exports as well as lowering imports

content.text: The tariffs may also be outside U.S. trade law, since a court noted that tariffs require congressional authority.
content.reason: Legal challenges can change the durability of a policy shock.

passages.source_excerpt: the court for the federal district noted that tariffs should originate in Congress

content.text: Coming auto import swings will reflect timing around tariff relief, as front-running did earlier, rather than underlying demand.
content.reason: Anticipated tariff changes shift the timing of imports and can masquerade as real demand effects.

passages.source_excerpt: expect a big dip in September as European and Japanese importers wait for the finalization of their “deals”
